\section{Setup}

\textbf{Machine.} All numbers come from one laptop: an Intel Core i7-13700H (14 physical, 20
logical cores) with 15.75\,GB of RAM, running Windows 11 (build 26200). Software: Python 3.11.17,
FAISS 1.14.3 (faiss-cpu), numpy 2.4.6 and OpenBLAS 0.3.34. HNSW is FAISS's
\texttt{IndexHNSWFlat}, and index builds use 20 threads.
% SOURCE: results/env.json (os "Windows-10-10.0.26200-SP0": Python 3.11 reports Windows 11 as
% "Windows-10"; build 26200 >= 22000 is Windows 11), config.py (BUILD_THREADS)

\textbf{Data.} SIFT has 1,000,000 base vectors ($d{=}128$) and GloVe-100 has 1,183,514
($d{=}100$). GloVe vectors are L2-normalised, so Euclidean order equals angular order. Each
dataset has 10,000 queries: the first 5,000 are for tuning and the last 5,000 for reporting.
% SOURCE: results/part1_agreement.json, config.py (TUNE, TEST)

\textbf{Recall.} Recall@10 is tie-aware. A returned id is correct if its true squared distance
is at most $d_{10}(1+\epsilon)+\epsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}$, where $d_{10}$ is the 10th exact
neighbour's distance, $\epsilon=10^{-5}$ and $\epsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}=10^{-6}$. Duplicate and $-1$
ids are ignored, and recall is $\min(\#\text{correct},10)/10$ averaged over queries. Distances are
recomputed from the vectors in float64, never taken from the index. Ground truth is our own exact
top-100. The function has 11 unit tests.
% SOURCE: annbench/metrics.py, config.py (RECALL_*), tests/test_recall.py

\textbf{Protocol.}
\begin{itemize}
\item QPS is measured one query per call on a single thread (one FAISS and one BLAS thread),
  pinned to a performance core.
\item Each measurement is one warm-up pass plus 3 timed passes; we report the median.
\item Tuning uses the first 2,000 tune queries. An operating point at a target recall is the
  fastest config whose \emph{tune} recall reaches it; its \emph{test} recall and QPS are reported
  as measured.
\item A sweep stops after two consecutive points with test recall $\ge$0.999.
\item Before each sweep, a fixed exact search (200 queries on 20,000 vectors) is timed as a
  canary for machine-state drift.
\end{itemize}
% SOURCE: config.py (PIN_CPU, REPEATS, WARMUP, TUNE_N, EARLY_STOP_*, CANARY_*), annbench/timing.py

\section{Part 1: Exact baseline}
\input{../results/tables/part1_compact.tex}

\textbf{Agreement.} Our exact top-10 sets match the file for 99.35\% of SIFT queries and every
GloVe query (Table~\ref{tab:part1c}). All 65 SIFT mismatches are ties at the 10th distance, which
SIFT's integer coordinates make common. With ties allowed, recall against the file is 1.0000 on
both datasets, in both directions. The file's distances match ours to a relative
$1.2\times10^{-7}$ on SIFT and $1.6\times10^{-7}$ on GloVe.
% SOURCE: results/part1_agreement.json, results/tables/part1_compact.tex

\textbf{Single query vs batch.} On one thread, one batch call is 11.1$\times$ (SIFT) and
10.1$\times$ (GloVe) faster than one query per call.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Batch:} FAISS turns a batch into one matrix--matrix product (BLAS GEMM). Each base
  vector is loaded once and reused from cache for many queries, with SIMD-friendly blocking.
\item \emph{One at a time:} each query is a matrix--vector product. It re-streams every base
  vector (512\,B on SIFT) from RAM, so it is memory-bandwidth bound, and it also pays a per-call
  overhead.
\end{itemize}
With 20 threads the batch reaches 761\,QPS on SIFT but only 383 on GloVe; we did not find out why.
% SOURCE: results/tables/part1_compact.tex, results/tables/part1.tex (761, 383),
% results/tables/part2_cost.tex (512 B/vector)

\section{Part 2: HNSW, IVF-Flat and IVF-PQ}

\textbf{What was run.}
\begin{itemize}
\item HNSW: $M\in\{16,32,48\}$, sweeping efSearch up to 512.
\item IVF-Flat: nlist $\in\{1024,4096,8192\}$, sweeping nprobe up to 512.
\item IVF-PQ: nlist $\in\{1024,4096\}$ with 8-bit codes, $m\in\{16,32,64\}$ (SIFT) or
  $\{20,25,50\}$ (GloVe).
\item Two GloVe sweeps that never reached 0.95 were extended to 1024.
\end{itemize}
Figure~\ref{fig:part2} shows each index's best trade-off curve, and Table~\ref{tab:part2c} the
operating points at 0.95.
% SOURCE: config.py (GRIDS, SWEEP_EXTEND)

\begin{figure*}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.49\textwidth]{part2_sift.pdf}\hfill
\includegraphics[width=0.49\textwidth]{part2_glove.pdf}
\caption{Recall@10 (test) vs single-thread QPS (log): Pareto curve per index over all build
settings; dashed line: exact search.}
\label{fig:part2}
\end{figure*}
\input{../results/tables/part2_compact.tex}

\textbf{Results.} HNSW is the fastest index at 0.95 on both datasets: 155$\times$ exact search on
SIFT and 15$\times$ on GloVe, against 55$\times$ and 9$\times$ for IVF-Flat. The order is the same
at 0.90 (Table~\ref{tab:part2c}): 279$\times$ and 98$\times$ exact on SIFT, 36$\times$ and
29$\times$ on GloVe.
% SOURCE: results/tables/part2_qps.tex (speed-ups), results/tables/part2_compact.tex (QPS at 0.90 and 0.95)

\textbf{Why IVF-PQ fails.} IVF-PQ never reaches 0.90 (Table~\ref{tab:part2c}). It ranks
candidates by distances computed on quantised codes, and that quantisation error does not depend
on nprobe. When the true 10th and 11th neighbours are closer together than the error, they are
mis-ordered whatever nprobe is. Only exact re-ranking can fix this (Part 3).
% SOURCE: results/tables/part2_compact.tex, results/part2_notes.md

\section{Part 3: Compression on SIFT}

\textbf{Experiment.} With nlist${}=4096$ and 8-bit codes, we vary the number of PQ sub-vectors
$m\in\{8,16,32,64\}$. Each $m$ is swept in two variants: plain IVF-PQ, and the \emph{same}
trained index wrapped in \texttt{IndexRefineFlat}, which re-ranks the top 100 candidates with
exact distances. The hypothesis was committed before the run.
% SOURCE: config.py (PART3), hypothesis.md

\begin{figure*}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.86\textwidth]{part3.pdf}
\caption{Part 3. Left: recall vs QPS per $m$ (solid: plain; dashed: exact re-rank of the top
100). Right: bytes per vector vs best recall.}
\label{fig:part3}
\end{figure*}
\input{../results/tables/part3_compact.tex}

\textbf{Results} (Figure~\ref{fig:part3}, Table~\ref{tab:part3c}).
\begin{itemize}
\item Plain IVF-PQ's recall ceiling rises with $m$ but never reaches 0.90.
\item Re-ranking lifts it to 0.95 or above for $m\ge16$.
\item At the same nprobe, re-ranking costs a factor of 1.09 to 1.29 in QPS (median by $m$), and at
  most 1.42.
\item The price is memory: re-ranking keeps the raw float32 vectors in RAM, about 512\,B on top of
  the PQ part. That erases most of PQ's saving, unless the vectors are read from disk, which we
  did not test.
\end{itemize}
% SOURCE: results/tables/part3_compact.tex, results/part3_notes.md, results/tables/part2_cost.tex (512)

\section{Part 4: Drifting data (own data)}

\textbf{What changed.}
\begin{itemize}
\item Indexes are built on SIFT base vectors 0--200K.
\item Vectors 200K--400K are then added, moved by $s\cdot R\cdot u$. Here $u$ is a fixed random
  unit direction (seed 42) and $R=383.2$ is the base vectors' mean distance to their centroid.
\item 2,000 queries (1,000 tune, 1,000 test) get the same shift. Only $s$ changes:
  $s\in\{0.25,0.5,1\}$, plus the control $s=0$, for 400K vectors in total.
\item \emph{Stale} indexes (trained or built on the base, then extended) are compared with
  \emph{rebuilt} ones (built on all 400K), for IVF-Flat (nlist 1024) and HNSW ($M{=}32$).
  Ground truth is recomputed for every shift.
\end{itemize}
% SOURCE: config.py (PART4, SEED), results/results.csv (part=4, extra.R), annbench/synth.py

\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{part4.pdf}
\caption{QPS at recall 0.95 vs shift. Solid: rebuilt; dashed, hollow: stale.}
\label{fig:part4}
\end{figure}
\input{../results/tables/part4_compact.tex}

\textbf{What happened} (Figure~\ref{fig:part4}, Table~\ref{tab:part4c}).
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Stale IVF-Flat slows down as $s$ grows.} From $s=0$ to $s=1$, its list-size CV rises
  from 0.44 to 0.76 and the longest list from 3.1 to 8.6 times the mean. The share of added vectors
  in the largest 1\% of lists rises from 3\% to 9\%. At $s=1$ it needs 18,842 distance
  computations per query against 12,693 for rebuilt, and reaches only 0.66 of rebuilt's QPS.
  Recall stays above 0.95, so the damage is to speed.
\item \emph{HNSW is unaffected:} stale and rebuilt are within a QPS ratio of 0.99 to 1.04 at every
  shift. Inserting the shifted vectors took 7.3 to 10.8\,s, against 16.9 to 19.9\,s to rebuild.
\item \emph{The dip at $s=0.25$ is a grid step, not drift:} both HNSW variants needed efSearch 48
  instead of 32.
\end{itemize}
% SOURCE: results/tables/part4_compact.tex, results/tables/part4.tex (max/mean, top-1%, times,
% efSearch at s=0.25), results/part4_notes.md (ratios)

\textbf{Mechanism.}
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{IVF:} centroids are frozen at training. Shifted vectors pile into the few cells
  nearest the new region, and the shifted queries probe exactly those long lists, so each probe
  scans more vectors. Retraining moves centroids into the new region and rebalances the lists.
\item \emph{HNSW:} nothing is trained. Each inserted vector links to its nearest neighbours as it
  arrives, so the graph adapts.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Hypothesis.}
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Supported:}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item the control behaves the same stale and rebuilt (QPS ratio 0.98 for IVF, 1.01 for HNSW);
  \item IVF imbalance grows with $s$, and the damage is to speed, not recall;
  \item rebuilt IVF stays within 1.00--1.14$\times$ of the control;
  \item HNSW is robust.
  \end{itemize}
\item \emph{Not supported:} the size of the effect. I predicted at least a 2$\times$ IVF
  slowdown at $s=1$; it was 1.5$\times$.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{Not tested:} rotations, deletions, new clusters, IVF-PQ, shifts beyond $1.0R$, other
nlist and $M$, and old-distribution queries after drift.
% SOURCE: results/part4_notes.md, hypothesis.md

\section{Answers}

\textbf{Q1. Fastest at 0.95.} HNSW is fastest on both datasets (Table~\ref{tab:part2c}), so the
winner does not change between datasets, but the cost does. On GloVe both indexes are far slower,
and HNSW needs a larger graph and wider search ($M{=}32$, efSearch 384 instead of $M{=}16$,
efSearch 64).
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Why HNSW wins:} its greedy graph walk moves to ever-closer neighbours, so it computes
  few distances. IVF scans whole inverted lists, most of which are far from the query. On Part 4's
  400K vectors at 0.95, HNSW computed 914--1,337 distances per query against 12,693--18,842 for
  IVF-Flat.
\item \emph{Why GloVe is harder (not measured):} GloVe's nearest neighbours are likely barely
  closer than many other vectors, so both indexes must examine more candidates.
\end{itemize}
% SOURCE: results/tables/part2_compact.tex, results/tables/part4.tex (distances per query)

\textbf{Q2. Cost; what PQ saves and gives up.} Table~\ref{tab:part2c} gives build time and
memory.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Build time:} HNSW is slowest on GloVe, because every insertion runs a search with
  efConstruction 200 to find its links. IVF's time is mostly k-means training (13.5 of 18.9\,s on
  SIFT, and 51.7 of IVF-PQ's 62.3\,s, which adds PQ codebooks).
\item \emph{Memory:} HNSW stores the raw vectors plus about $2M$ neighbour ids, so it needs more
  than the raw 512 or 400\,B per vector. IVF-Flat is the raw vectors plus an 8-byte id.
\item \emph{What PQ saves:} it keeps only an $m$-byte code, so SIFT IVF-PQ takes 18.3 to
  74.3\,B per vector.
\item \emph{What PQ gives up:} accuracy, a ceiling of 0.885 on SIFT and 0.863 on GloVe. Getting
  recall back by re-ranking puts the raw vectors back in RAM (Table~\ref{tab:part3c}).
\end{itemize}
% SOURCE: results/tables/part2_compact.tex, results/tables/part2_cost.tex (train s, raw B),
% results/tables/part3_compact.tex

\textbf{Q3. Parts 3 and 4.} Part 3 against my hypothesis:
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Supported:}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item plain IVF-PQ is capped, and the cap rises with $m$ ($m{=}8$: 0.412, below my 0.60;
    $m{=}16$: 0.590, below my 0.90);
  \item re-ranking reaches 0.95 for $m\ge16$, while $m{=}8$ falls short (0.885), as allowed;
  \item re-ranking costs under 2$\times$ in QPS;
  \item memory was within my estimates (18.3--74.3 vs 16--72\,B predicted).
  \end{itemize}
\item \emph{Wrong:}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item $m{=}64$ did not ``come close to 0.95'' (0.885);
  \item larger $m$ cost far more than ``slightly'': re-rank QPS at 0.95 fell from 2,917
    ($m{=}16$) to 1,067 ($m{=}64$).
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
Part 4 held in direction (control, IVF damage, recovery by rebuilding, robust HNSW) but not in
size: the IVF slowdown at $s=1$ was 1.5$\times$, not 2$\times$.

\emph{When headline numbers mislead:}
\begin{itemize}
\item a PQ ``bytes per vector'' figure means little without the recall it reaches, because the
  compact index cannot reach 0.95 and the index that can is no longer compact;
\item headline QPS comes from indexes built on the data they serve. Under drift, an extended IVF
  index is slower than Part 2 suggests, while HNSW is not.
\end{itemize}
% SOURCE: hypothesis.md, results/part3_notes.md, results/tables/part3_compact.tex,
% results/part4_notes.md

\input{../results/tables/q4_compact.tex}
\textbf{Q4. 150K or 10M vectors, 100\,ms, 16\,GB} (Table~\ref{tab:q4c}).
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{150K: no ANN is needed.} Measured exact search takes 4.5 and 3.3\,ms with recall 1.0.
  The linear model from the 1M timings predicted 4.87 and 3.69\,ms, so latency scales about
  linearly with $n$. ANN pays off only if throughput matters.
\item \emph{10M: use HNSW.} Exact search is \emph{projected} at 324.9 and 245.8\,ms, because
  every query scans all vectors. Memory is not the problem: the raw vectors alone take 4.77 and
  3.73\,GiB, so exact search fails on latency, not RAM. HNSW at the measured 0.95 settings is
  \emph{extrapolated} to 0.24 and 2.22\,ms, since its search grows roughly with $\log n$. It needs
  6.11 and 6.26\,GiB, which fits.
\item \emph{Caveats at 10M:}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item building needs the raw vectors and the graph in RAM at once (about 10.9 and 10.0\,GiB);
  \item build time extrapolates to about 12 and 24\,min, optimistically;
  \item efSearch must rise to hold 0.95 (not measured);
  \item IVF-PQ with re-ranking from disk is the fallback if memory is tight.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
% SOURCE: results/tables/q4_compact.tex, results/tables/q4.tex (raw GiB 4.77 / 3.73), results/q4_notes.md

\textbf{Q5. How this benchmark could mislead.}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Machine-state drift (tested, not corrected).}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The overnight canary varied by 21.3\% (SIFT) and 23.3\% (GloVe).
  \item Power state matters too: the quick pipeline ran much slower on battery than plugged in
    (see the README).
  \item Pinning and medians cut noise within a measurement, not across hours. Part 4's
    close-in-time control agreed within 2\%.
  \end{itemize}
\item \emph{``Batch'' speed is a library heuristic (tested).}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item FAISS 1.14.3 uses BLAS only when queries $\times\,d\ge$128,000.
  \item A single-thread batch over 100K GloVe vectors ran at 216\,QPS with 1,279 queries but
    1,306 with 1,280 (timed on battery; recall 1.0000 for both).
  \item Our 5,000-query batches are above the threshold.
  \end{itemize}
\item \emph{Single thread, one machine (not tested elsewhere).} 20 threads helped SIFT batches
  (761 vs 342\,QPS) far more than GloVe (383 vs 348). Rankings under multi-threaded serving or on
  other CPUs are untested.
\item \emph{Tune/test split (tested).} The $|$test${}-{}$tune$|$ recall gap has a median of
  0.0147 (SIFT) and 0.0043 (GloVe), at most 0.0500. GloVe HNSW $M{=}16$/efSearch 1024 reaches
  0.9527 on test but 0.9490 on tune, so it does not count as reaching 0.95.
\item \emph{Tie tolerance (partly tested).} 65 SIFT queries tie at the 10th neighbour, so a
  tie-blind check scores exact search at 0.9935 instead of 1.0000. Ties are unit-tested;
  sensitivity to $\epsilon$ is not.
\end{enumerate}
